addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact can declare — calling the user's claude.ai connectors (MCP) from the page, and future abilities. Load this BEFORE passing `capabilities` to the Artifact tool or writing any `window.claude.mcp` code.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

This is a Python security log analysis tool (trace-log-sec) that's mid-refactor (files being moved from flat layout into src/config, src/engine, src/models, src/cli, src/tests).

   - Which functions/classes/modules it targets (import paths)

Also note any obvious gaps you notice while reading (e.g. a source function with multiple branches but only one test). Be thorough — read full file contents, not just grep matches. This is research only, do not modify anything.

<result>Confirmed: `auth_incidents.log` and `webserver_incidents.log` are consumed only by `scripts/run_demo.py` (a manual demo script), not by any pytest test. Now I have everything needed for the report.

## Test Suite Map: `src/tests/`

**Files present:** `__init__.py` (empty), `test_correlation.py`, `test_engine.py`, `test_parsers.py`, `test_rules.py`, `fixtures/` (`auth.log`, `webserver.log`, `auth_incidents.log`, `webserver_incidents.log`, `incidents_manifest.md`). No `conftest.py` anywhere in the repo.

---

### 1. `src/tests/test_correlation.py`
**Targets:** `engine.correlation.Correlator` (imports `from engine.correlation import Correlator`, `from models import Finding, Severity`)

| Test | Scenario | Verifies |
|---|---|---|
| `test_two_rules_same_ip_form_incident` | SUCCESS | Two different rules firing on same IP within window merge into 1 incident with 2 findings |
| `test_single_rule_repeats_never_form_incident` | FAILURE/edge | Same rule repeating for one IP never forms an incident (requires diversity) |
| `test_two_sources_same_rule_form_incident` | SUCCESS | Same rule but two different `sources` (auth/webserver) still merges into an incident |
| `test_findings_outside_window_do_not_cluster` | FAILURE/edge | Findings 1h apart (outside correlation window) do not cluster |
| `test_severity_escalation_cap` | SUCCESS | HIGH + HIGH escalates to CRITICAL (capped, doesn't overflow past top) |
| `test_severity_escalation_medium_to_high` | SUCCESS | MEDIUM + MEDIUM escalates one level to HIGH |
| `test_incident_id_deterministic` | SUCCESS | Same input findings produce the same `incident_id` twice, prefixed `INC-` |
| `test_findings_without_ip_are_ignored` | FAILURE/edge | Findings with `ip=None` are excluded from correlation entirely |

**Gap:** No test for 3+ rules/incidents on the same IP, no test mixing multiple distinct IPs in one call (isolation across IPs), and no direct test of severity escalation from LOW or at max ceiling (only MEDIUM→HIGH and HIGH→CRITICAL are exercised — no CRITICAL+CRITICAL "already at cap" case).

---

### 2. `src/tests/test_engine.py`
**Targets:** `engine.Engine`, `engine.LogSource`, `engine.correlation.Correlator`, `engine.parsers.{CombinedLogParser, LogParser, SyslogAuthParser}`, `engine.rules.{ThresholdRule, build_rules}`, `config.settings.{load_settings, rule_specs}`, `models.{AuthLogEntry, AuthOutcome, Severity, WebLogEntry}`

Defines a local `ListParser(LogParser)` test double and helpers `write_lines`, `make_auth_log`, `make_web_log`, `config_rules()` (builds the real default rule set from `config.yaml`).

| Test | Scenario | Verifies |
|---|---|---|
| `test_end_to_end_correlated_incident` | SUCCESS (E2E) | Full pipeline: auth SSH brute force + web login brute force from same IP → both rule findings fire and correlate into 1 CRITICAL incident |
| `test_stats_shape` | SUCCESS | `report.stats` dict shape: `sources`/`totals`/`duration_seconds` keys, per-source counters, totals include findings/incidents |
| `test_missing_file_captured_not_raised` | FAILURE | Non-strict mode: missing file produces a `parse_errors` entry (line_no=0) instead of raising, findings empty |
| `test_missing_file_strict_raises` | FAILURE | `strict=True` mode: missing file raises `FileNotFoundError` |
| `test_all_malformed_file_is_normal_report` | FAILURE | File where every line is malformed → 0 findings, 2 parse_errors, stats reflect malformed count, no crash |
| `test_empty_file_is_normal_report` | FAILURE/edge | Empty file → empty findings, empty parse_errors (no error at all) |
| `test_engine_rerun_idempotent` | SUCCESS | Running `.analyze()` twice on the same source yields identical finding counts (no shared mutable state leak) |
| `test_ordering_stateful_rule_sees_only_its_own_source_order` | SUCCESS/invariant | A stateful `ThresholdRule` matching only `auth_failure` isn't disturbed by interleaved webserver source processed first — verifies ordering invariants I1/I2 from docs §8 |

**Gap:** No test using the real `auth_incidents.log`/`webserver_incidents.log` fixtures (all engine tests build synthetic tiny logs via `tmp_path`) — the rich, documented incident fixtures with `incidents_manifest.md` are entirely unused by the automated suite. No test for `Engine` with zero `LogSource`s, no test for a `LogSource` list with duplicate paths, and no direct unit test of `LogSource` itself.

---

### 3. `src/tests/test_parsers.py`
**Targets:** `engine.parsers.{CombinedLogParser, MalformedLineError, SyslogAuthParser, parse_file}`, `models.{AuthOutcome, ParseError, WebLogEntry}`

**Combined/Common access log parsing (`CombinedLogParser`):**
| Test | Scenario | Verifies |
|---|---|---|
| `test_combined_full_line` | SUCCESS | Full combined-format line parses every field correctly (ip, user, method, target, protocol, status, size, referrer, UA, timestamp with tz) |
| `test_common_line_no_referrer_agent_and_dash_size` | SUCCESS/edge | Common log format (no referrer/UA fields): `-` → `size=0`, `referrer=None`, `user_agent=None`, `user=None` |
| `test_target_keeps_query_string_and_props` | SUCCESS | `target` retains full query string; `path`/`query` properties split correctly |
| `test_garbage_request_line_is_best_effort_not_error` | FAILURE/edge (soft) | A malformed request-line string (`"GARBAGE"`) is parsed best-effort (method="GARBAGE", target=None) rather than raising |
| `test_malformed_combined_raises` | FAILURE | Totally unparseable line raises `MalformedLineError` |
| `test_bad_timestamp_raises` | FAILURE | Line with an invalid date (`99/Zzz/2025`) raises `MalformedLineError` |

**Syslog auth log parsing (`SyslogAuthParser`):**
| Test | Scenario | Verifies |
|---|---|---|
| `test_auth_failure_outcome_and_fields` | SUCCESS | "Failed password" line → outcome=FAILURE, username, source_ip, port, process, pid all extracted |
| `test_invalid_user_outcome` | SUCCESS | "Failed password for invalid user X" → outcome=INVALID_USER |
| `test_accepted_is_success` | SUCCESS | "Accepted publickey" → outcome=SUCCESS |
| `test_preauth_is_other_but_extracts_ip` | SUCCESS/edge | "Connection closed ... [preauth]" → outcome=OTHER but IP/port still extracted |
| `test_year_heuristic_picks_prior_year_for_future_date` | SUCCESS/edge | Year-inference heuristic picks prior year when computed date would be in the future relative to reference time |
| `test_year_heuristic_uses_current_year_for_past_date` | SUCCESS/edge | Year-inference heuristic picks current year when date is in the past relative to reference |
| `test_default_year_override` | SUCCESS | Explicit `default_year` param overrides heuristic entirely |
| `test_malformed_auth_raises` | FAILURE | Unparseable auth line raises `MalformedLineError` |

**Streaming file parse (`parse_file`):**
| Test | Scenario | Verifies |
|---|---|---|
| `test_parse_file_mixes_entries_and_errors_and_counts` | SUCCESS+FAILURE mixed | Mixed file (good line, blank line, malformed line, good line) yields correct entries/errors split and counters (`lines_read`, `skipped_blank`) |
| `test_parse_file_missing_file_yields_source_level_error` | FAILURE | Nonexistent path yields a single source-level `ParseError` with `line_no=0`, not a raised exception |

**Gap:** No dedicated test for `Failed password` with `invalid user` combined with an unusual port/malformed port number; no test of `SyslogAuthParser` line with a non-integer PID or missing PID; no test of `CombinedLogParser` IPv6 addresses; no test of `parse_file` where the parser itself is `SyslogAuthParser` (only `CombinedLogParser` is exercised in `parse_file` tests).

---

**`MalformedLineError(Exception)`** — carries `.reason`; raised by parsers on unparseable lines/timestamps.

**`class LogParser(ABC)`** — abstract; `parse_line(line, line_no) -> LogEntry`, must raise `MalformedLineError` on failure.

**`CombinedLogParser.parse_line`** (NCSA Combined access log)
- Regex mismatch → raises `MalformedLineError("does not match Combined log format")`.
- `datetime.strptime` on the time group can raise `ValueError` — **caught** and re-raised as `MalformedLineError`.

Still a latent gap: if the regex is ever loosened, this becomes an uncaught `ValueError`.
- `_split_request` — pure best-effort `.split()`, never raises; returns `None` for missing fields, so a garbage request line just silently degrades method/target/protocol to `None,None,None` rather than failing the whole line. This is a deliberate silent-degradation design choice, not a bug, but worth flagging: callers of `method`/`target`/`protocol` downstream (rules match on `target`) must all tolerate `None`.
- `_dash_to_none` — trivial, no failure mode.

**`SyslogAuthParser.parse_line`** (BSD syslog auth.log)
- Regex mismatch → `MalformedLineError("does not match BSD syslog format")`.
- `_resolve_timestamp`: `int(day)` inside an f-string passed to `strptime` — `int(day)` **is not wrapped**; the regex guarantees `day` is `\d{1,2}` so it can't fail today, but again fragile-by-construction rather than defensively caught. The `strptime` call itself **is** wrapped and converted to `MalformedLineError`.

- `pid_raw` → `int(pid_raw) if pid_raw else None`; regex constrains pid to `\d+` so safe.
- `_classify_auth`: pure regex-search based, never raises; ambiguous/unmatched messages just fall through to `AuthOutcome.OTHER, None, ip, port` — silent classification degradation, by design, not an exception.

**`parse_file(path, parser, *, counters=None) -> Iterator[LogEntry | ParseError]`**
- File open wrapped in `try/except OSError` → yields a single `ParseError` with `line_no=0` (a "source-level" error, e.g. missing file, permission denied, is-a-directory). This is the **only** point where "file doesn't exist / unreadable" is handled, and it converts it to data rather than raising — callers must explicitly check `line_no == 0` to detect this (which `Engine.analyze` does, but only when `strict=True`; see below).
- Non-`OSError` exceptions during `path.open()` (e.g. none realistically expected, but also nothing guards against, say, a `MemoryError` or a non-str/Path `path` argument causing a `TypeError` before `Path(path)` even succeeds) — `Path(path)` itself isn't wrapped; a bad type passed as `path` would raise **uncaught** `TypeError`.

- `MalformedLineError` from `parser.parse_line` → converted to `ParseError`; anything else the parser might raise (e.g. an unexpected `AttributeError`/`IndexError` from a buggy custom parser) is **not caught** here — would propagate out of `parse_file` and up through `Engine.analyze`, aborting the whole run. This is an explicit gap: only `MalformedLineError` is treated as "expected/recoverable"; any other exception type from a parser plugin is fatal engine-wide.

## 2. `src/engine/correlation.py` — `Correlator`

- `correlate(findings)`: groups by `f.source_ip` (via `defaultdict`), `ip=None` group is explicitly skipped ("can't meaningfully correlate findings with no IP") — handled, not an error.
- Assumes every `Finding` has valid `first_seen`/`last_seen`/`severity`/`rule_id`/`sources` attributes populated — **no defensive checks**; if a caller ever constructs a `Finding` with `first_seen > last_seen`, or an empty `sources` set, nothing here validates it (rule code always sets them consistently today, but the correlator has zero guardrails of its own).
- `_cluster`: greedy clustering assumes findings are pre-sorted by `first_seen` (done by caller just before). If `_cluster` were ever called directly with unsorted input, the "current_end" tracking would degrade silently (not raise, just produce wrong/too-many clusters) — a **silent correctness bug**, not a crash, on out-of-order input if a future caller forgets to sort first.
- `_build_incident`: `min(f.first_seen for f in cluster)` / `max(f.last_seen ...)` / `max(f.severity for f in cluster)` — all called on `cluster`, which is guaranteed non-empty by construction (`_cluster` never appends empty lists), so no `ValueError: min() arg is an empty sequence` risk today, but it's implicit, not asserted — a future refactor of `_cluster` that could yield an empty cluster would break this silently/loudly.
- `_escalate`: `members.index(max_severity)` — `Severity` is a closed `IntEnum` so `max_severity` will always be a member; safe.
- `hashlib.sha1(...)` on a string built from `ip`, `first_seen.isoformat()`, sorted `rule_ids` — no failure mode, though note `ip` here is typed `str` in the signature but the `by_ip` dict key can genuinely be `None` in theory (guarded by the `if ip is None: continue` above, so fine in practice).
- No I/O, no dict/list indexing of external/untrusted data structures beyond `Finding` attributes assumed always-present (dataclass-enforced).

## 3. `src/engine/engine.py` — `Engine`

Flow: reset rules → for each `LogSource`, stream `parse_file` → route `ParseError` vs `LogEntry` → feed entries to every rule's `inspect()` → after all sources, call every rule's `flush()` → trim evidence to `max_evidence` → correlate → build stats dict → return `AnalysisReport`.

Error handling:
- `ParseError` with `line_no == 0` (source-level, e.g. missing/unreadable file) is only escalated to a raised `FileNotFoundError` if `self.strict=True`; otherwise it's appended to `parse_errors` and logged via `logger.warning`, and the loop just continues (0 entries parsed for that source, stats show 0s). **Non-strict mode never raises for a missing file** — silent-by-design, verified by `test_missing_file_captured_not_raised`.
- `rule.inspect(item)` is called with **no exception handling at all** — if any rule implementation raises (bug in a custom/config-driven rule, or a `KeyError`/`AttributeError` from unexpected entry data), the whole `analyze()` call aborts uncaught. Same for `rule.flush()`. This is a real gap: a single misbehaving rule (or a rule from a bad config that doesn't match the entry types it receives) takes down the entire multi-source run, unlike parse errors which are isolated.
- Evidence trimming: `del f.evidence[self.max_evidence:]` — safe even if `max_evidence <= 0` or evidence shorter than cap.
- Empty file: yields nothing (blank-only or literally 0 lines) → normal empty report, no error (covered by `test_empty_file_is_normal_report`).
- No timeout/size guard on files — a huge file streams line-by-line so it's memory-safe, but a rule holding growing per-IP state (e.g. `ThresholdRule._events`) is unbounded across an entire run except by its own window eviction logic — no engine-level cap on number of distinct IPs tracked (potential unbounded-memory issue with attacker-controlled/spoofed source IPs, not strictly "error handling" but adjacent).
- `_build_stats`: assumes every `per_source` stats dict has all four keys (`lines_read/parsed/malformed/skipped_blank`) — guaranteed since `Engine.analyze` always seeds them via `setdefault` before use, so safe in practice; would `KeyError` if `per_source` were ever populated by a bypassing caller instead.

## 4. Rules and rule config loading

**`src/engine/rules/factory.py` — `build_rules(specs)`**
- `spec.get("enabled", True)` — safe.
- `type_name = spec.get("type")`; if not in `RULE_TYPES` → raises **generic `ValueError`** (`f"unknown rule type {type_name!r} for id {spec.get('id')!r}"`) — this propagates uncaught out of `build_rules` to whatever called it (in `run_demo.py`, straight out of `main()`, killing the script with a traceback; no CLI wraps this yet since `src/cli` is unimplemented).
- `kwargs["id"] = spec["id"]` — **raw dict indexing, not `.get()`**. If a spec dict is missing the `"id"` key entirely, this raises an uncaught `KeyError` with no context message (unlike the `type` check, which validates first and gives a friendly error). This is an inconsistency: `type` is validated with a clear error, `id` is not validated at all before being force-indexed.
- `cls(**kwargs)` — if `params` in config contains extra/misspelled keys, or is missing required constructor args (e.g. `ThresholdRule` requires `match`, `threshold`, `window_seconds` with no defaults; `PatternSignatureRule` requires `patterns`), Python raises **uncaught `TypeError`** (missing required positional-or-keyword arg / unexpected keyword arg) with a fairly opaque message and no indication of which config rule id caused it (well, the id is in kwargs, but the TypeError message itself won't mention it).
- `_coerce_severity`: for a string calls `Severity.from_name` (raises `ValueError` on unknown name — this one **is** wrapped by `Severity.from_name` into a clear message); for a non-Severity, non-str value calls `Severity(value)` — if `value` is e.g. a float or unmapped int, raises uncaught `ValueError: ... is not a valid Severity`.
- **No duplicate-id detection**: nothing in `build_rules` checks for repeated `spec["id"]` values across the specs list. The comment header in `config.yaml` explicitly claims "Supplying a rule with an existing id overrides it" — **this is not actually implemented** anywhere in `factory.py`/`settings.py`. Two specs with the same `id` will just produce two separate `Rule` instances with the same `.id`, both run independently, and downstream correlation/reporting will have two findings tagged with the same `rule_id` — a **documentation/behavior mismatch** worth flagging directly, since it looks like a claimed feature that silently doesn't exist.

**`src/engine/rules/registry.py`** — trivial decorator-based registration into a module-level dict; no failure modes (registration always succeeds; lookups are done by the factory, which handles the miss case).

**`src/engine/rules/utils.py` — `resolve_preset`** — looks up `presets[name]`; on `KeyError` raises `ValueError(f"unknown {kind} {name!r}")` — clean and always used at rule-construction time (`ThresholdRule.__init__` calls it for `match` and `distinct_by`; `PatternSignatureRule.__init__` calls it for `target`). So an unknown `match`/`distinct_by`/`target` string in config.yaml raises immediately when the rule is constructed inside `build_rules` — uncaught by `build_rules` itself, propagates same as the `TypeError` cases above.

**`src/engine/rules/signature.py` — `PatternSignatureRule`**
- `re.compile(p, flags)` in `__init__` for every pattern string in config — **completely unguarded**; an invalid regex in `config.yaml` (e.g. unbalanced parens) raises uncaught `re.error` at rule-construction time, again inside `build_rules`, with no rule-id context added.
- `_decode_variants`: `unquote(current, errors="replace")` — explicitly fail-soft (`errors="replace"` means bad percent-escapes never raise); bounded by `MAX_DECODE_PASSES=2` so no infinite loop risk even on pathological repeatedly-encoded input. Good defensive design here.
- `inspect`: `getattr(e, "target", None)` style extractors always return `None` rather than raising for the wrong entry type — safe.
- `flush()`: no failure modes; just filters by `min_hits`.

**`src/engine/rules/threshold.py` — `ThresholdRule`**
- Constructor takes `threshold: int`, `window_seconds: float` with **no validation** — a config with `threshold: 0` or `threshold: -5` or `window_seconds: -60` will construct successfully and then produce nonsensical behavior at runtime (e.g. `threshold <= 0` means `count < self.threshold` is basically never true, so it fires on the very first event of every burst; negative `window_seconds` creates a `timedelta` that makes `cutoff > right_edge`, evicting everything immediately, effectively disabling the rule) — **silent misconfiguration, not an exception**, could easily hide a broken detection rule with no error/warning at all.
- Out-of-order timestamp handling *is* explicitly designed for (`right_edge = max(...)` rather than assuming input order) — this is a deliberate correctness feature, not a gap, and is documented in the docstring/comment (§6.3).
- `window[0]` access in the `while` eviction loop — safe, guarded by `while window and ...`.
- No division, no indexing that can go out of bounds.

**`src/config/settings.py`**
- `load_settings(path)`: `open(path, encoding="utf-8")` — **no try/except at all**. A missing `config.yaml` (bad custom path, or the packaged default file somehow absent/corrupted install) raises an uncaught `FileNotFoundError`/`OSError`. Similarly a directory-permission issue raises `PermissionError` uncaught.
- `yaml.safe_load(f)` — **no try/except**. Malformed YAML (bad indentation, unclosed quotes, etc.) raises uncaught `yaml.YAMLError` (specifically `yaml.scanner.ScannerError`/`ParserError`).
- If the YAML parses but is `None` (e.g. an empty file) or a list/scalar instead of a mapping, `EngineSettings.model_validate(data)` — pydantic will raise a `pydantic.ValidationError` for `None`/wrong-shape input; this **is somewhat handled** by virtue of pydantic validation, but it's an uncaught `ValidationError` propagating out of `load_settings`, not translated into a friendlier engine-level error. No code anywhere catches `ValidationError`.
- Missing required keys (e.g. a rule spec missing `type`) → pydantic `ValidationError` (uncaught, but at least structured/informative — much better than the raw `KeyError`/`TypeError` failure modes in `build_rules`).
- Wrong types for `id`/`type` (e.g. `id: 123` as YAML int) — pydantic v2 by default coerces reasonably (int→str via lax mode is actually **not** allowed for `str` fields in pydantic v2 strict-ish default — it does allow int-to-str coercion in lax mode actually) — regardless, if coercion fails, `ValidationError`, uncaught here.

- `src/cli/__init__.py` contains only a docstring `"""Command-line interface for trace-log-sec (to be implemented)."""` — **no CLI code exists at all**. There is no arg-parsing, no error handling to evaluate here yet; this is a pure placeholder.
- `scripts/run_demo.py` (explicitly documented as "not the CLI"):

  - `engine = Engine(build_rules(rule_specs(load_settings())))` — **completely unguarded**.   - Print loops (`sorted(report.findings, key=lambda f: (-f.severity, ...))`) — `-f.severity` relies on `Severity` being an `IntEnum` (confirmed), so negation works; no failure mode.

## 6. Cross-cutting summary of raw dict/list indexing, `.split()`, regex-group access, file I/O, and type casts

| Location | Operation | Guarded? |
|---|---|---|
| `engine/parsers.py: CombinedLogParser.parse_line` | `int(status_raw)`, `int(size_raw)` | Not directly try/excepted, but regex-constrained so effectively safe today |
| `engine/parsers.py: SyslogAuthParser._resolve_timestamp` | `int(day)`, `datetime.strptime(...)` | strptime wrapped → `MalformedLineError`; `int(day)` not wrapped but regex-constrained |
| `engine/parsers.py: SyslogAuthParser.parse_line` | `int(pid_raw)` | Not wrapped; regex-constrained (`\d+`) so safe today |
| `engine/parsers.py: _classify_auth` | `int(fm.group("port"))`, `int(pm.group("port"))` | Not wrapped; regex-constrained (`\d+`) so safe today |
| `engine/parsers.py: _split_request` | `.split()` on request string | Fully guarded — never raises, degrades gracefully |
| `engine/parsers.py: parse_file` | `path.open(...)` | `OSError` caught → `ParseError`; other exception types (e.g. bad `path` type before `Path()` conversion) not caught |
| `config/settings.py: load_settings` | `open(path)`, `yaml.safe_load(f)` | **Not caught at all** — biggest gap in the whole codebase |
| `engine/rules/factory.py: build_rules` | `spec["id"]` (raw indexing) | **Not caught** — `KeyError` propagates raw |
| `engine/rules/factory.py: build_rules` | `cls(**kwargs)` | **Not caught** — `TypeError` for missing/unexpected rule params propagates raw, no rule-id context |
| `engine/rules/factory.py: _coerce_severity` | `Severity(value)` | Not caught — raw `ValueError` for bad non-string severity values |
| `engine/rules/signature.py: PatternSignatureRule.__init__` | `re.compile(p, flags)` | **Not caught** — raw `re.error` for invalid regex patterns from config |
| `engine/rules/utils.py: resolve_preset` | dict lookup `presets[name]` | Caught, re-raised as clear `ValueError` |
| `engine/engine.py: Engine.analyze` | `rule.inspect(item)`, `rule.flush()` | **Not caught at all** — any rule bug/exception aborts the whole multi-source run |
| `engine/correlation.py` | `min()/max()` over cluster | Implicitly safe only because `_cluster` never yields empty lists; not defensively asserted |

### Highest-value gaps for the "error-handling" evaluation
1. **`config/settings.py: load_settings`** has zero error handling for file-not-found, permission errors, malformed YAML, or empty/wrong-shaped YAML — and is completely untested (no `test_settings.py`).
2. **`engine/rules/factory.py: build_rules`** raises raw, inconsistent, low-context exceptions (`KeyError` for missing `id`, `TypeError` for bad/missing rule constructor params, `re.error` for bad regex patterns, `ValueError` for bad severities/unknown presets) — none of these are caught anywhere up the call chain, and none of the messages include which config entry/file caused the failure except the one deliberate `ValueError` for unknown `type`.
3. **Duplicate rule `id` values** are silently accepted at both the pydantic (`settings.py`) and factory (`build_rules`) layers despite `config.yaml`'s own header comment claiming duplicate ids "override" — a real behavior/doc mismatch, not just a missing-error-handling gap.
4. **`engine/engine.py: Engine.analyze`** treats parse errors as fully recoverable/isolated per-line, but a single rule raising any exception during `inspect()`/`flush()` is fatal to the entire run across all sources — asymmetric robustness between the parsing layer (very defensive) and the rule-execution layer (not defensive at all).
5. **`ThresholdRule`** silently accepts nonsensical config values (`threshold <= 0`, negative `window_seconds`) with no validation, producing wrong detection behavior with no error or warning.
6. **`scripts/run_demo.py`** has no try/except around config/rule loading, so any of the above config-driven failures crash it with a raw traceback — acceptable for a dev smoke-test script per its own docstring, but relevant since `src/cli` (the real entry point) doesn't exist yet and will need to handle all of this itself.</result>

- `_split_request` — pure best-effort `.split()`, never raises; returns `None` for missing fields, so a garbage request line just silently degrades method/target/protocol to `None,None,None` rather than failing the whole line. This is a deliberate silent-degradation design choice, not a bug, but worth flagging: callers of `method`/`target`/`protocol` downstream (rules match on `target`) must all tolerate `None`.
- `_dash_to_none` — trivial, no failure mode.

**`SyslogAuthParser.parse_line`** (BSD syslog auth.log)
- Regex mismatch → `MalformedLineError("does not match BSD syslog format")`.
- `_resolve_timestamp`: `int(day)` inside an f-string passed to `strptime` — `int(day)` **is not wrapped**; the regex guarantees `day` is `\d{1,2}` so it can't fail today, but again fragile-by-construction rather than defensively caught. The `strptime` call itself **is** wrapped and converted to `MalformedLineError`.
  - Year-rollback edge case: `candidate.replace(year=ref.year - 1)` can raise `ValueError` only for Feb-29 in a non-leap prior year; that specific case **is** handled (falls back to day=28). No other `replace()` failure mode is possible for month/day already validated by strptime.
- `pid_raw` → `int(pid_raw) if pid_raw else None`; regex constrains pid to `\d+` so safe.
- `_classify_auth`: pure regex-search based, never raises; ambiguous/unmatched messages just fall through to `AuthOutcome.OTHER, None, ip, port` — silent classification degradation, by design, not an exception.

**`parse_file(path, parser, *, counters=None) -> Iterator[LogEntry | ParseError]`**
- File open wrapped in `try/except OSError` → yields a single `ParseError` with `line_no=0` (a "source-level" error, e.g. missing file, permission denied, is-a-directory). This is the **only** point where "file doesn't exist / unreadable" is handled, and it converts it to data rather than raising — callers must explicitly check `line_no == 0` to detect this (which `Engine.analyze` does, but only when `strict=True`; see below).
- Non-`OSError` exceptions during `path.open()` (e.g. none realistically expected, but also nothing guards against, say, a `MemoryError` or a non-str/Path `path` argument causing a `TypeError` before `Path(path)` even succeeds) — `Path(path)` itself isn't wrapped; a bad type passed as `path` would raise **uncaught** `TypeError`.
- Blank lines are skipped silently (counted in `counters["skipped_blank"]`).
- `MalformedLineError` from `parser.parse_line` → converted to `ParseError`; anything else the parser might raise (e.g. an unexpected `AttributeError`/`IndexError` from a buggy custom parser) is **not caught** here — would propagate out of `parse_file` and up through `Engine.analyze`, aborting the whole run. This is an explicit gap: only `MalformedLineError` is treated as "expected/recoverable"; any other exception type from a parser plugin is fatal engine-wide.

## 2. `src/engine/correlation.py` — `Correlator`

- `correlate(findings)`: groups by `f.source_ip` (via `defaultdict`), `ip=None` group is explicitly skipped ("can't meaningfully correlate findings with no IP") — handled, not an error.
- Assumes every `Finding` has valid `first_seen`/`last_seen`/`severity`/`rule_id`/`sources` attributes populated — **no defensive checks**; if a caller ever constructs a `Finding` with `first_seen > last_seen`, or an empty `sources` set, nothing here validates it (rule code always sets them consistently today, but the correlator has zero guardrails of its own).
- `_cluster`: greedy clustering assumes findings are pre-sorted by `first_seen` (done by caller just before). If `_cluster` were ever called directly with unsorted input, the "current_end" tracking would degrade silently (not raise, just produce wrong/too-many clusters) — a **silent correctness bug**, not a crash, on out-of-order input if a future caller forgets to sort first.
- `_build_incident`: `min(f.first_seen for f in cluster)` / `max(f.last_seen ...)` / `max(f.severity for f in cluster)` — all called on `cluster`, which is guaranteed non-empty by construction (`_cluster` never appends empty lists), so no `ValueError: min() arg is an empty sequence` risk today, but it's implicit, not asserted — a future refactor of `_cluster` that could yield an empty cluster would break this silently/loudly.
- `_escalate`: `members.index(max_severity)` — `Severity` is a closed `IntEnum` so `max_severity` will always be a member; safe.
- `hashlib.sha1(...)` on a string built from `ip`, `first_seen.isoformat()`, sorted `rule_ids` — no failure mode, though note `ip` here is typed `str` in the signature but the `by_ip` dict key can genuinely be `None` in theory (guarded by the `if ip is None: continue` above, so fine in practice).
- No I/O, no dict/list indexing of external/untrusted data structures beyond `Finding` attributes assumed always-present (dataclass-enforced).

## 3. `src/engine/engine.py` — `Engine`

Flow: reset rules → for each `LogSource`, stream `parse_file` → route `ParseError` vs `LogEntry` → feed entries to every rule's `inspect()` → after all sources, call every rule's `flush()` → trim evidence to `max_evidence` → correlate → build stats dict → return `AnalysisReport`.

Error handling:
- `ParseError` with `line_no == 0` (source-level, e.g. missing/unreadable file) is only escalated to a raised `FileNotFoundError` if `self.strict=True`; otherwise it's appended to `parse_errors` and logged via `logger.warning`, and the loop just continues (0 entries parsed for that source, stats show 0s). **Non-strict mode never raises for a missing file** — silent-by-design, verified by `test_missing_file_captured_not_raised`.
- `rule.inspect(item)` is called with **no exception handling at all** — if any rule implementation raises (bug in a custom/config-driven rule, or a `KeyError`/`AttributeError` from unexpected entry data), the whole `analyze()` call aborts uncaught. Same for `rule.flush()`. This is a real gap: a single misbehaving rule (or a rule from a bad config that doesn't match the entry types it receives) takes down the entire multi-source run, unlike parse errors which are isolated.
- Evidence trimming: `del f.evidence[self.max_evidence:]` — safe even if `max_evidence <= 0` or evidence shorter than cap.
- Empty file: yields nothing (blank-only or literally 0 lines) → normal empty report, no error (covered by `test_empty_file_is_normal_report`).
- No timeout/size guard on files — a huge file streams line-by-line so it's memory-safe, but a rule holding growing per-IP state (e.g. `ThresholdRule._events`) is unbounded across an entire run except by its own window eviction logic — no engine-level cap on number of distinct IPs tracked (potential unbounded-memory issue with attacker-controlled/spoofed source IPs, not strictly "error handling" but adjacent).
- `_build_stats`: assumes every `per_source` stats dict has all four keys (`lines_read/parsed/malformed/skipped_blank`) — guaranteed since `Engine.analyze` always seeds them via `setdefault` before use, so safe in practice; would `KeyError` if `per_source` were ever populated by a bypassing caller instead.

## 4. Rules and rule config loading

**`src/engine/rules/factory.py` — `build_rules(specs)`**
- `spec.get("enabled", True)` — safe.
- `type_name = spec.get("type")`; if not in `RULE_TYPES` → raises **generic `ValueError`** (`f"unknown rule type {type_name!r} for id {spec.get('id')!r}"`) — this propagates uncaught out of `build_rules` to whatever called it (in `run_demo.py`, straight out of `main()`, killing the script with a traceback; no CLI wraps this yet since `src/cli` is unimplemented).
- `kwargs["id"] = spec["id"]` — **raw dict indexing, not `.get()`**. If a spec dict is missing the `"id"` key entirely, this raises an uncaught `KeyError` with no context message (unlike the `type` check, which validates first and gives a friendly error). This is an inconsistency: `type` is validated with a clear error, `id` is not validated at all before being force-indexed.
- `cls(**kwargs)` — if `params` in config contains extra/misspelled keys, or is missing required constructor args (e.g. `ThresholdRule` requires `match`, `threshold`, `window_seconds` with no defaults; `PatternSignatureRule` requires `patterns`), Python raises **uncaught `TypeError`** (missing required positional-or-keyword arg / unexpected keyword arg) with a fairly opaque message and no indication of which config rule id caused it (well, the id is in kwargs, but the TypeError message itself won't mention it).
- `_coerce_severity`: for a string calls `Severity.from_name` (raises `ValueError` on unknown name — this one **is** wrapped by `Severity.from_name` into a clear message); for a non-Severity, non-str value calls `Severity(value)` — if `value` is e.g. a float or unmapped int, raises uncaught `ValueError: ... is not a valid Severity`.
- **No duplicate-id detection**: nothing in `build_rules` checks for repeated `spec["id"]` values across the specs list. The comment header in `config.yaml` explicitly claims "Supplying a rule with an existing id overrides it" — **this is not actually implemented** anywhere in `factory.py`/`settings.py`. Two specs with the same `id` will just produce two separate `Rule` instances with the same `.id`, both run independently, and downstream correlation/reporting will have two findings tagged with the same `rule_id` — a **documentation/behavior mismatch** worth flagging directly, since it looks like a claimed feature that silently doesn't exist.

**`src/engine/rules/registry.py`** — trivial decorator-based registration into a module-level dict; no failure modes (registration always succeeds; lookups are done by the factory, which handles the miss case).

**`src/engine/rules/utils.py` — `resolve_preset`** — looks up `presets[name]`; on `KeyError` raises `ValueError(f"unknown {kind} {name!r}")` — clean and always used at rule-construction time (`ThresholdRule.__init__` calls it for `match` and `distinct_by`; `PatternSignatureRule.__init__` calls it for `target`). So an unknown `match`/`distinct_by`/`target` string in config.yaml raises immediately when the rule is constructed inside `build_rules` — uncaught by `build_rules` itself, propagates same as the `TypeError` cases above.

**`src/engine/rules/signature.py` — `PatternSignatureRule`**
- `re.compile(p, flags)` in `__init__` for every pattern string in config — **completely unguarded**; an invalid regex in `config.yaml` (e.g. unbalanced parens) raises uncaught `re.error` at rule-construction time, again inside `build_rules`, with no rule-id context added.
- `_decode_variants`: `unquote(current, errors="replace")` — explicitly fail-soft (`errors="replace"` means bad percent-escapes never raise); bounded by `MAX_DECODE_PASSES=2` so no infinite loop risk even on pathological repeatedly-encoded input. Good defensive design here.
- `inspect`: `getattr(e, "target", None)` style extractors always return `None` rather than raising for the wrong entry type — safe.
- `flush()`: no failure modes; just filters by `min_hits`.

**`src/engine/rules/threshold.py` — `ThresholdRule`**
- Constructor takes `threshold: int`, `window_seconds: float` with **no validation** — a config with `threshold: 0` or `threshold: -5` or `window_seconds: -60` will construct successfully and then produce nonsensical behavior at runtime (e.g. `threshold <= 0` means `count < self.threshold` is basically never true, so it fires on the very first event of every burst; negative `window_seconds` creates a `timedelta` that makes `cutoff > right_edge`, evicting everything immediately, effectively disabling the rule) — **silent misconfiguration, not an exception**, could easily hide a broken detection rule with no error/warning at all.
- Out-of-order timestamp handling *is* explicitly designed for (`right_edge = max(...)` rather than assuming input order) — this is a deliberate correctness feature, not a gap, and is documented in the docstring/comment (§6.3).
- `window[0]` access in the `while` eviction loop — safe, guarded by `while window and ...`.
- No division, no indexing that can go out of bounds.

**`src/config/settings.py`**
- `load_settings(path)`: `open(path, encoding="utf-8")` — **no try/except at all**. A missing `config.yaml` (bad custom path, or the packaged default file somehow absent/corrupted install) raises an uncaught `FileNotFoundError`/`OSError`. Similarly a directory-permission issue raises `PermissionError` uncaught.
- `yaml.safe_load(f)` — **no try/except**. Malformed YAML (bad indentation, unclosed quotes, etc.) raises uncaught `yaml.YAMLError` (specifically `yaml.scanner.ScannerError`/`ParserError`).
- If the YAML parses but is `None` (e.g. an empty file) or a list/scalar instead of a mapping, `EngineSettings.model_validate(data)` — pydantic will raise a `pydantic.ValidationError` for `None`/wrong-shape input; this **is somewhat handled** by virtue of pydantic validation, but it's an uncaught `ValidationError` propagating out of `load_settings`, not translated into a friendlier engine-level error. No code anywhere catches `ValidationError`.
- Missing required keys (e.g. a rule spec missing `type`) → pydantic `ValidationError` (uncaught, but at least structured/informative — much better than the raw `KeyError`/`TypeError` failure modes in `build_rules`).
- Wrong types for `id`/`type` (e.g. `id: 123` as YAML int) — pydantic v2 by default coerces reasonably (int→str via lax mode is actually **not** allowed for `str` fields in pydantic v2 strict-ish default — it does allow int-to-str coercion in lax mode actually) — regardless, if coercion fails, `ValidationError`, uncaught here.
- Duplicate rule `id`s across the YAML list: pydantic performs **no uniqueness validation** on `list[RuleSpec]` — same duplicate-id gap noted above, now confirmed it isn't caught at the settings layer either.
- `rule_specs(settings)`: trivial `model_dump(exclude_none=True)` per rule, no failure modes.
- **No test file exists for `settings.py`** (`src/tests/` has no `test_settings.py`) — confirmed via `find`; none of the above malformed-config paths (missing file, bad YAML syntax, missing required key, wrong type, duplicate id) have any test coverage today.

## 5. `src/cli/` and `scripts/run_demo.py`

- `src/cli/__init__.py` contains only a docstring `"""Command-line interface for trace-log-sec (to be implemented)."""` — **no CLI code exists at all**. There is no arg-parsing, no error handling to evaluate here yet; this is a pure placeholder.
- `scripts/run_demo.py` (explicitly documented as "not the CLI"):
  - `main(argv)`: only accepts `len(argv) == 1` (defaults) or `== 3` (auth+web path); any other arg count prints `__doc__` and returns exit code `2` — reasonable minimal validation, but it doesn't validate that the two paths actually point to real files before use; it just passes them straight to `LogSource`.
  - `_reference_time(web_path)`: calls `parse_file(web_path, CombinedLogParser())` directly (bypassing `Engine`) purely to find the latest timestamp. If `web_path` doesn't exist, `parse_file` yields a single `ParseError` (per its documented crash-proof behavior) and the `for` loop simply does nothing (no `WebLogEntry` instances to compare), so `latest` stays `None` and falls back to `datetime.now(UTC)` — silent, no error surfaced to the user at this stage (the missing-file problem only becomes visible later when `Engine.analyze` runs and appends it to `report.parse_errors`, printed in the "PARSE ERRORS" section — so this recovers gracefully, but the *reference date* silently becomes "today" rather than warning the user their auth-log year resolution is now anchored on `now()` instead of log data).
  - `engine = Engine(build_rules(rule_specs(load_settings())))` — **completely unguarded**. Any of the config-loading/rule-building failure modes above (missing/malformed `config.yaml`, bad regex, unknown rule type, missing `id` key, invalid `threshold`/severity value) will raise an uncaught exception here and crash the script with a raw Python traceback before any log analysis even starts. No try/except anywhere in `run_demo.py`.
  - `report.stats["totals"]` — raw dict indexing assumed always present; safe today since `Engine._build_stats` always populates it, but if `Engine.analyze` were ever call to fail partway (e.g. rule raises inside the loop, per the gap noted above), `main()` never gets a `report` object at all and this line is moot — the crash happens earlier.
  - Print loops (`sorted(report.findings, key=lambda f: (-f.severity, ...))`) — `-f.severity` relies on `Severity` being an `IntEnum` (confirmed), so negation works; no failure mode.

## 6. Cross-cutting summary of raw dict/list indexing, `.split()`, regex-group access, file I/O, and type casts

| Location | Operation | Guarded? |
|---|---|---|
| `engine/parsers.py: CombinedLogParser.parse_line` | `int(status_raw)`, `int(size_raw)` | Not directly try/excepted, but regex-constrained so effectively safe today |
| `engine/parsers.py: SyslogAuthParser._resolve_timestamp` | `int(day)`, `datetime.strptime(...)` | strptime wrapped → `MalformedLineError`; `int(day)` not wrapped but regex-constrained |
| `engine/parsers.py: SyslogAuthParser.parse_line` | `int(pid_raw)` | Not wrapped; regex-constrained (`\d+`) so safe today |
| `engine/parsers.py: _classify_auth` | `int(fm.group("port"))`, `int(pm.group("port"))` | Not wrapped; regex-constrained (`\d+`) so safe today |
| `engine/parsers.py: _split_request` | `.split()` on request string | Fully guarded — never raises, degrades gracefully |
| `engine/parsers.py: parse_file` | `path.open(...)` | `OSError` caught → `ParseError`; other exception types (e.g. bad `path` type before `Path()` conversion) not caught |
| `config/settings.py: load_settings` | `open(path)`, `yaml.safe_load(f)` | **Not caught at all** — biggest gap in the whole codebase |
| `engine/rules/factory.py: build_rules` | `spec["id"]` (raw indexing) | **Not caught** — `KeyError` propagates raw |
| `engine/rules/factory.py: build_rules` | `cls(**kwargs)` | **Not caught** — `TypeError` for missing/unexpected rule params propagates raw, no rule-id context |
| `engine/rules/factory.py: _coerce_severity` | `Severity(value)` | Not caught — raw `ValueError` for bad non-string severity values |
| `engine/rules/signature.py: PatternSignatureRule.__init__` | `re.compile(p, flags)` | **Not caught** — raw `re.error` for invalid regex patterns from config |
| `engine/rules/utils.py: resolve_preset` | dict lookup `presets[name]` | Caught, re-raised as clear `ValueError` |
| `engine/engine.py: Engine.analyze` | `rule.inspect(item)`, `rule.flush()` | **Not caught at all** — any rule bug/exception aborts the whole multi-source run |
| `engine/correlation.py` | `min()/max()` over cluster | Implicitly safe only because `_cluster` never yields empty lists; not defensively asserted |

### Highest-value gaps for the "error-handling" evaluation
1. **`config/settings.py: load_settings`** has zero error handling for file-not-found, permission errors, malformed YAML, or empty/wrong-shaped YAML — and is completely untested (no `test_settings.py`).
2. **`engine/rules/factory.py: build_rules`** raises raw, inconsistent, low-context exceptions (`KeyError` for missing `id`, `TypeError` for bad/missing rule constructor params, `re.error` for bad regex patterns, `ValueError` for bad severities/unknown presets) — none of these are caught anywhere up the call chain, and none of the messages include which config entry/file caused the failure except the one deliberate `ValueError` for unknown `type`.
3. **Duplicate rule `id` values** are silently accepted at both the pydantic (`settings.py`) and factory (`build_rules`) layers despite `config.yaml`'s own header comment claiming duplicate ids "override" — a real behavior/doc mismatch, not just a missing-error-handling gap.
4. **`engine/engine.py: Engine.analyze`** treats parse errors as fully recoverable/isolated per-line, but a single rule raising any exception during `inspect()`/`flush()` is fatal to the entire run across all sources — asymmetric robustness between the parsing layer (very defensive) and the rule-execution layer (not defensive at all).
5. **`ThresholdRule`** silently accepts nonsensical config values (`threshold <= 0`, negative `window_seconds`) with no validation, producing wrong detection behavior with no error or warning.
6. **`scripts/run_demo.py`** has no try/except around config/rule loading, so any of the above config-driven failures crash it with a raw traceback — acceptable for a dev smoke-test script per its own docstring, but relevant since `src/cli` (the real entry point) doesn't exist yet and will need to handle all of this itself.</result>

"""Loads and validates the YAML rule configuration.

Kept outside the ``engine`` package so the core detection engine stays
format-agnostic (it only ever sees structured specs — plain dicts — never a
file path or a YAML/pydantic dependency). See docs/rule-config-plan.md.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel
import yaml

from constants import DEFAULT_CONFIG_FILENAME

PACKAGE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
DEFAULT_CONFIG_PATH = PACKAGE_DIR / DEFAULT_CONFIG_FILENAME


class RuleSpec(BaseModel):
    id: str
    type: str
    enabled: bool = True
    severity: str | None = None
    params: dict[str, Any] = {}


class EngineSettings(BaseModel):
    rules: list[RuleSpec]


def load_settings(path: str | Path = DEFAULT_CONFIG_PATH) -> EngineSettings:
    """Read and validate the YAML config at ``path``."""
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        data = yaml.safe_load(f)
    return EngineSettings.model_validate(data)


def rule_specs(settings: EngineSettings) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    """Convert validated rule specs into the plain dicts ``build_rules`` expects."""
    return [r.model_dump(exclude_none=True) for r in settings.rules]

1	"""Factory that turns structured config specs into ``Rule`` instances."""
2	
3	from __future__ import annotations
4	
5	from collections.abc import Iterable
6	from typing import Any
7	
8	from engine.rules.base import Rule
9	from engine.rules.registry import RULE_TYPES
10	from models import Severity
11	
12	
13	def build_rules(specs: Iterable[dict[str, Any]]) -> list[Rule]:
14	    """Instantiate rules from structured specs (list of dicts).
15	
16	    Each spec: ``{id, type, enabled?, severity?, params?}``. ``severity`` (top
17	    level) and everything in ``params`` are merged into the rule constructor.
18	    Disabled specs are skipped. Format loading (YAML/TOML) lives outside core.
19	    """
20	    rules: list[Rule] = []
21	    for spec in specs:
22	        if not spec.get("enabled", True):
23	            continue
24	        type_name = spec.get("type")
25	        if type_name not in RULE_TYPES:
26	            raise ValueError(f"unknown rule type {type_name!r} for id {spec.get('id')!r}")
27	        cls = RULE_TYPES[type_name]
28	
29	        kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {"id": spec["id"]}
30	        if "severity" in spec:
31	            kwargs["severity"] = _coerce_severity(spec["severity"])
32	        for key, value in spec.get("params", {}).items():
33	            kwargs[key] = _coerce_severity(value) if key == "severity" else value
34	        rules.append(cls(**kwargs))
35	    return rules
36	
37	
38	def _coerce_severity(value: Any) -> Severity:  # noqa: ANN401 (genuinely dynamic: parsed config data)
39	    if isinstance(value, Severity):
40	        return value
41	    if isinstance(value, str):
42	        return Severity.from_name(value)
43	    return Severity(value)
44

6	
7	See docs/engine-plan.md §8.

11

15	from typing import Any

18	from models import AnalysisReport, Finding, Incident, LogSource, ParseError

21	from .parsers import parse_file
22	from .rules import Rule

25	class Engine:
26	    """Orchestrates parsing → detection → correlation over a set of sources."""
27	
28	    def __init__(
29	        self,
30	        rules: Sequence[Rule],
31	        *,
32	        correlator: Correlator | None = None,
33	        logger: logging.Logger | None = None,
34	        max_evidence: int = DEFAULT_MAX_EVIDENCE,
35	        strict: bool = False,
36	    ) -> None:
37	        self.rules = list(rules)
38	        self.correlator = correlator if correlator is not None else Correlator()
39	        self.logger = logger or logging.getLogger("trace_log_sec.engine")
40	        self.max_evidence = max_evidence
41	        self.strict = strict
42	
43	    def analyze(self, sources: Iterable[LogSource]) -> AnalysisReport:
44	        started = time.monotonic()
45	
46	        # 0. Reset every rule so a single Engine is safely re-runnable.
47	        for rule in self.rules:
48	            rule.reset()
49

"""Engine orchestration.

Feeds parsed entries through every rule, flushes end-of-stream aggregates, and
runs the correlator. Never crashes on bad input: parse failures (including a
missing file) are captured as ``ParseError`` unless ``strict=True``.

See docs/engine-plan.md §8.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Iterable, Sequence
import logging
import time
from typing import Any

from constants import DEFAULT_MAX_EVIDENCE
from models import AnalysisReport, Finding, Incident, LogSource, ParseError

from .correlation import Correlator
from .parsers import parse_file
from .rules import Rule


class Engine:
    """Orchestrates parsing → detection → correlation over a set of sources."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        rules: Sequence[Rule],
        *,
        correlator: Correlator | None = None,
        logger: logging.Logger | None = None,
        max_evidence: int = DEFAULT_MAX_EVIDENCE,
        strict: bool = False,
    ) -> None:
        self.rules = list(rules)
        self.correlator = correlator if correlator is not None else Correlator()
        self.logger = logger or logging.getLogger("trace_log_sec.engine")
        self.max_evidence = max_evidence
        self.strict = strict

    def analyze(self, sources: Iterable[LogSource]) -> AnalysisReport:
        started = time.monotonic()

        # 0. Reset every rule so a single Engine is safely re-runnable.
        for rule in self.rules:
            rule.reset()

        findings: list[Finding] = []
        parse_errors: list[ParseError] = []
        per_source: dict[str, dict[str, int]] = {}

        for source in sources:
            stats = per_source.setdefault(
                source.path,
                {"lines_read": 0, "parsed": 0, "malformed": 0, "skipped_blank": 0},
            )
            for item in parse_file(source.path, source.parser, counters=stats):
                if isinstance(item, ParseError):
                    if item.line_no == 0 and self.strict:
                        raise FileNotFoundError(item.reason)
                    parse_errors.append(item)
                    self.logger.warning(
                        "parse error in %s line %d: %s",
                        item.source,
                        item.line_no,
                        item.reason,
                    )
                    if item.line_no > 0:
                        stats["malformed"] += 1
                    continue

                stats["parsed"] += 1
                for rule in self.rules:
                    findings.extend(rule.inspect(item))

        # 4. Flush end-of-stream aggregates.
        for rule in self.rules:
            findings.extend(rule.flush())

        # Cap evidence to the engine-wide ceiling. A rule's own max_evidence
        # (if lower) already wins during collection; this only trims further.
        for f in findings:
            if len(f.evidence) > self.max_evidence:
                del f.evidence[self.max_evidence :]

        # 5. Correlate.
        incidents = self.correlator.correlate(findings)

        stats = self._build_stats(per_source, findings, incidents, started)
        return AnalysisReport(
            findings=findings,
            incidents=incidents,
            parse_errors=parse_errors,
            stats=stats,
        )

    @staticmethod
    def _build_stats(
        per_source: dict[str, dict[str, int]],
        findings: list[Finding],
        incidents: list[Incident],
        started: float,
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        totals = {
            "lines_read": 0,
            "parsed": 0,
            "malformed": 0,
            "skipped_blank": 0,
            "findings": len(findings),
            "incidents": len(incidents),
        }
        for s in per_source.values():
            for key in ("lines_read", "parsed", "malformed", "skipped_blank"):
                totals[key] += s[key]
        return {
            "sources": per_source,
            "totals": totals,
            "duration_seconds": time.monotonic() - started,
        }

1	"""Threshold rule: stateful per-IP sliding window (brute force, scanning, ...).
2	
3	Fires one finding per burst that crosses the configured threshold.
4	See docs/engine-plan.md §6.
5	"""
6	
7	from __future__ import annotations
8	
9	from collections import deque
10	from collections.abc import Iterable
11	from datetime import datetime, timedelta
12	
13	from constants import DEFAULT_MAX_EVIDENCE
14	from engine.rules.base import Rule
15	from engine.rules.registry import register
16	from engine.rules.utils import FieldExtractor, Predicate, add_evidence, resolve_preset
17	from models import AuthLogEntry, AuthOutcome, Finding, LogEntry, Severity, WebLogEntry
18	
19	# Named predicates (the config-safe "match" presets).
20	
21	
22	def _auth_failure(entry: LogEntry) -> bool:
23	    return isinstance(entry, AuthLogEntry) and entry.outcome in (AuthOutcome.FAILURE, AuthOutcome.INVALID_USER)
24	
25	
26	def _web_login_failure(entry: LogEntry) -> bool:
27	    # A failed request (401/403) to a login-shaped endpoint — deliberately
28	    # narrower than "any 401/403", which would also catch admin-path probing
29	    # (a different signal, not login brute force).
30	    if not isinstance(entry, WebLogEntry) or entry.status not in (401, 403):
31	        return False
32	    path = entry.path
33	    return path is not None and "login" in path.lower()
34	
35	
36	def _web_404(entry: LogEntry) -> bool:
37	    return isinstance(entry, WebLogEntry) and entry.status == 404
38	
39	
40	MATCH_PREDICATES: dict[str, Predicate] = {
41	    "auth_failure": _auth_failure,
42	    "web_login_failure": _web_login_failure,
43	    "web_404": _web_404,
44	}
45	
46	
47	# Named field extractors for `distinct_by` — also a config-safe preset set.
48	
49	
50	def _distinct_path(entry: LogEntry) -> str | None:
51	    """Normalized path key: no query, trailing slash trimmed (except root)."""
52	    if not isinstance(entry, WebLogEntry) or entry.path is None:
53	        return None
54	    path = entry.path
55	    if len(path) > 1:
56	        path = path.rstrip("/") or "/"
57	    return path
58	
59	
60	def _distinct_username(entry: LogEntry) -> str | None:
61	    return entry.username if isinstance(entry, AuthLogEntry) else None
62	
63	
64	DISTINCT_EXTRACTORS: dict[str, FieldExtractor] = {
65	    "path": _distinct_path,
66	    "username": _distinct_username,
67	}
68	
69	
70	@register("threshold")
71	class ThresholdRule(Rule):
72	    """Per-IP sliding window; fires one finding per burst that crosses threshold."""
73	
74	    def __init__(
75	        self,
76	        *,
77	        id: str,
78	        match: str,
79	        threshold: int,
80	        window_seconds: float,
81	        severity: Severity = Severity.MEDIUM,
82	        distinct_by: str | None = None,
83	        title: str | None = None,
84	        description: str = "",
85	        max_evidence: int = DEFAULT_MAX_EVIDENCE,
86	    ) -> None:
87	        self.id = id
88	        self.title = title or id
89	        self.severity = severity
90	        self.description = description
91	        self.threshold = threshold
92	        self.window = timedelta(seconds=window_seconds)
93	        self.max_evidence = max_evidence
94	        self._match_name = match
95	        self._match = resolve_preset(match, MATCH_PREDICATES, "match preset")
96	        self._distinct_name = distinct_by
97	        self._distinct = resolve_preset(distinct_by, DISTINCT_EXTRACTORS, "distinct_by field") if distinct_by else None
98	        # Per-IP window state.
99	        self._events: dict[str | None, deque[LogEntry]] = {}
100	        self._active: dict[str | None, Finding] = {}
101	        self._max_seen: dict[str | None, datetime] = {}
102	
103	    def reset(self) -> None:
104	        self._events = {}
105	        self._active = {}
106	        self._max_seen = {}
107	
108	    def inspect(self, entry: LogEntry) -> Iterable[Finding]:
109	        if not self._match(entry):
110	            return ()
111	
112	        ip = entry.source_ip
113	        window = self._events.setdefault(ip, deque())
114	        window.append(entry)
115	
116	        # Evict events older than `window` relative to the right edge, which is
117	        # the max timestamp seen for this IP so far — not necessarily this
118	        # entry's own timestamp, since a single IP's events aren't guaranteed
119	        # to arrive in order (§6.3 out-of-order tolerance).
120	        right_edge = self._max_seen.get(ip)
121	        if right_edge is None or entry.timestamp > right_edge:
122	            right_edge = entry.timestamp
123	        self._max_seen[ip] = right_edge
124	        cutoff = right_edge - self.window
125	        while window and window[0].timestamp < cutoff:
126	            window.popleft()
127	
128	        count = self._count(window)
129	        if count < self.threshold:
130	            # Burst has subsided (or not yet begun): clear any active finding so
131	            # a later crossing starts a fresh one — one finding per burst.
132	            self._active.pop(ip, None)
133	            return ()
134	
135	        emitted = self._update_finding(ip, window, count, entry)
136	        return (emitted,) if emitted is not None else ()
137	
138	    def _count(self, window: deque[LogEntry]) -> int:
139	        if self._distinct is None:
140	            return len(window)
141	        values = {self._distinct(e) for e in window}
142	        values.discard(None)
143	        return len(values)
144	
145	    def _update_finding(self, ip: str | None, window: deque[LogEntry], count: int, entry: LogEntry) -> Finding | None:
146	        finding = self._active.get(ip)
147	        newly_emitted = finding is None
148	        if finding is None:
149	            finding = Finding(
150	                rule_id=self.id,
151	                title=self.title,
152	                severity=self.severity,
153	                description=self.description,
154	                first_seen=window[0].timestamp,
155	                last_seen=entry.timestamp,
156	                source_ip=ip,
157	                count=count,
158	                sources={entry.source},
159	                evidence=[],
160	                metadata={
161	                    "match": self._match_name,
162	                    "distinct_by": self._distinct_name,
163	                    "threshold": self.threshold,
164	                    "window_seconds": self.window.total_seconds(),
165	                },
166	            )
167	            self._active[ip] = finding
168	
169	        finding.count = count
170	        finding.last_seen = max(finding.last_seen, entry.timestamp)
171	        finding.sources.add(entry.source)
172	        add_evidence(finding, entry, self.max_evidence)
173	
174	        return finding if newly_emitted else None
175	
176	    def flush(self) -> Iterable[Finding]:
177	        # Findings are emitted eagerly on the crossing event; nothing buffered.
178	        return ()
179

1	"""Cross-rule correlation.
2	
3	Groups findings by IP and clusters those close in time into ``Incident``s. An
4	incident forms only for genuine multi-signal activity (≥2 distinct rules OR ≥2
5	sources for the same IP) — a single rule's repeated findings never do.
6	
7	See docs/engine-plan.md §7.
8	"""
9	
10	from __future__ import annotations
11	
12	from collections import defaultdict
13	from collections.abc import Iterable
14	from datetime import datetime, timedelta
15	import hashlib
16	
17	from constants import DEFAULT_CORRELATION_WINDOW_MINUTES
18	from models import Finding, Incident, Severity
19	
20	
21	class Correlator:
22	    """Stateless correlator; clusters findings per IP within a time window."""
23	
24	    def __init__(self, window: timedelta = timedelta(minutes=DEFAULT_CORRELATION_WINDOW_MINUTES)) -> None:
25	        self.window = window
26	
27	    def correlate(self, findings: Iterable[Finding]) -> list[Incident]:
28	        by_ip: dict[str | None, list[Finding]] = defaultdict(list)
29	        for f in findings:
30	            by_ip[f.source_ip].append(f)
31	
32	        incidents: list[Incident] = []
33	        for ip, ip_findings in by_ip.items():
34	            if ip is None:
35	                continue  # can't meaningfully correlate findings with no IP
36	            ip_findings.sort(key=lambda f: f.first_seen)
37	            for cluster in self._cluster(ip_findings):
38	                incident = self._build_incident(ip, cluster)
39	                if incident is not None:
40	                    incidents.append(incident)
41	
42	        incidents.sort(key=lambda i: (i.first_seen, i.source_ip or ""))
43	        return incidents
44	
45	    def _cluster(self, findings: list[Finding]) -> list[list[Finding]]:
46	        """Greedily group findings whose gap from the running span <= window."""
47	        clusters: list[list[Finding]] = []
48	        current: list[Finding] = []
49	        current_end: datetime | None = None
50	        for f in findings:
51	            if current_end is not None and f.first_seen - current_end <= self.window:
52	                current.append(f)
53	                current_end = max(current_end, f.last_seen)
54	            else:
55	                if current:
56	                    clusters.append(current)
57	                current = [f]
58	                current_end = f.last_seen
59	        if current:
60	            clusters.append(current)
61	        return clusters
62	
63	    def _build_incident(self, ip: str, cluster: list[Finding]) -> Incident | None:
64	        rule_ids = {f.rule_id for f in cluster}
65	        sources = {s for f in cluster for s in f.sources}
66	        if len(rule_ids) < 2 and len(sources) < 2:
67	            return None
68	
69	        first_seen = min(f.first_seen for f in cluster)
70	        last_seen = max(f.last_seen for f in cluster)
71	        severity = self._escalate(max(f.severity for f in cluster))
72	
73	        # sha1 for a short deterministic display id, not a security use of the hash.
74	        incident_id = (
75	            "INC-"
76	            + hashlib.sha1(  # noqa: S324
77	                (f"{ip}|{first_seen.isoformat()}|" + ",".join(sorted(rule_ids))).encode()
78	            ).hexdigest()[:10]
79	        )
80	
81	        return Incident(
82	            incident_id=incident_id,
83	            title=f"Correlated activity from {ip}",
84	            severity=severity,
85	            source_ip=ip,
86	            first_seen=first_seen,
87	            last_seen=last_seen,
88	            findings=list(cluster),
89	            narrative=self._narrative(ip, cluster, rule_ids, sources, first_seen, last_seen),
90	        )
91	
92	    @staticmethod
93	    def _escalate(max_severity: Severity) -> Severity:
94	        """One level above the max child severity, capped at CRITICAL."""
95	        members = sorted(Severity)
96	        idx = members.index(max_severity)
97	        return members[min(idx + 1, len(members) - 1)]
98	
99	    @staticmethod
100	    def _narrative(
101	        ip: str,
102	        cluster: list[Finding],
103	        rule_ids: set[str],
104	        sources: set[str],
105	        first_seen: datetime,
106	        last_seen: datetime,
107	    ) -> str:
108	        span = last_seen - first_seen
109	        titles = sorted({f.title for f in cluster})
110	        return (
111	            f"{ip} triggered {len(cluster)} findings across {len(rule_ids)} rule(s) "
112	            f"({', '.join(titles)}) over {', '.join(sorted(sources))} "
113	            f"within {span} ({first_seen.isoformat()} → {last_seen.isoformat()})."
114	        )

# Test coverage review + failure-scenario hardening plan

## Context

The repo is mid-refactor into a `src/` layout (`config`, `engine`, `models`, `cli`, `tests`) as part of "organizing the repository." Before that refactor solidifies, it's worth checking whether the test suite actually protects the new layout, and — since this is a security log analysis tool — whether it fails safely on the kind of input it's most likely to face in practice: broken configs, malformed logs, and buggy/misconfigured detection rules. A log analyzer that crashes instead of degrading is itself an availability/blind-spot risk (an attacker who can make one rule throw takes down detection for every other source in the run).

Two research passes (test-suite map + production-logic map) turned up a clear pattern: **the parsing layer (`engine/parsers.py`) is deliberately and thoroughly fail-soft, and it's well-tested for it.** Every other layer that touches untrusted/hand-authored input — `config/settings.py` (YAML loading), `engine/rules/factory.py` (rule construction from config), and `engine/engine.py`'s rule-execution loop — has little to no error handling and **zero** failure-scenario test coverage. That asymmetry is the main finding this plan addresses.

Success-scenario coverage is already strong (parsers, threshold/signature rules, correlation, end-to-end engine flow are all well exercised), so per the task instructions this plan focuses on the missing **failure scenarios** and the **code changes** needed to actually handle them, plus a short list of minor success-scenario gaps for completeness.

## Part A — Current coverage summary (for reference)

| File | Targets | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `test_parsers.py` | `CombinedLogParser`, `SyslogAuthParser`, `parse_file` | Strong; malformed lines, bad timestamps, missing files all covered. |
| `test_rules.py` | `ThresholdRule`, `PatternSignatureRule`, `build_rules` (happy path only) | Strong on rule *matching* logic; no failure-mode coverage for `build_rules`/config-driven construction. |
| `test_correlation.py` | `Correlator` | Good coverage of clustering/escalation/IP isolation. |
| `test_engine.py` | `Engine` end-to-end | Covers missing file (strict/non-strict), empty file, all-malformed file — but nothing about a rule that raises. |
| — | `config/settings.py` (`load_settings`) | **No test file exists at all.** |
| `fixtures/auth_incidents.log`, `webserver_incidents.log`, `incidents_manifest.md` | — | Rich, realistic, documented incident data — used only by `scripts/run_demo.py`, never by the automated suite. |

Minor success-scenario gaps worth picking up opportunistically (not the focus, low effort): an engine-level end-to-end test against the real `*_incidents.log` fixtures using `incidents_manifest.md` as the assertion source; a correlation test with 3+ IPs in one call; a `CRITICAL+CRITICAL` escalation-cap case.

## Part B — Failure scenarios (missing tests) → code fixes

Ordered by blast radius: a single bad rule spec or a single buggy rule can currently abort an entire multi-source analysis run with a raw, low-context Python exception. That's the core problem this plan fixes.

### 1. `config/settings.py::load_settings` — no error handling, no tests

**Missing scenarios:**
- Config file path doesn't exist → uncaught `FileNotFoundError`.
- Config file unreadable (permissions) → uncaught `PermissionError`.
- Malformed YAML syntax (bad indentation, unclosed quotes) → uncaught `yaml.YAMLError`.
- Empty file / YAML parses to `None` or a non-mapping (list, scalar) → uncaught `pydantic.ValidationError`.
- A rule entry missing a required key (`id` or `type`) → uncaught `pydantic.ValidationError` (informative, but untranslated).
- Two rule specs with the same `id` → **silently accepted as two separate rules**, even though the file's own header comment (`src/config/config.yaml:10`) documents that "supplying a rule with an existing id overrides it." This is a behavior/doc mismatch, not just a missing-error-handling case.

**Code fix (`src/config/settings.py`):**
- Wrap the `open()` + `yaml.safe_load()` calls in `try/except (OSError, yaml.YAMLError)` and re-raise as a single new `ConfigError(path, reason)` exception (small class local to `settings.py`) so callers get one consistent, informative error type instead of three raw ones.
- Wrap `EngineSettings.model_validate(data)` similarly, catching `pydantic.ValidationError` and re-raising as the same `ConfigError` with the path included (pydantic's own message already lists the offending field).
